notes: Pre-action disclosure in paediatric negligence context; balancing confidentiality and fair trial is detailed.

enrichment.short_title: Samuel R: pre-action disclosure against PCT in delayed Asperger's diagnosis claim
key_facts: A 10-year-old boy living with his maternal grandmother under a residence order had behavioural problems treated by the PCT from 1998 to 2002.
Asperger's Syndrome and ADHD were not diagnosed until July 2002, and a potential negligence claim was contemplated.
The PCT gave partial disclosure but resisted full records because of Samuel's therapy confidentiality and sensitive information about his mother.
The grandmother sought pre-action disclosure under CPR 31.16 to assess whether a claim had proper foundation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for pre-action disclosure under section 33(2) of the Supreme Court Act 1981 and CPR 31.16 before anticipated clinical negligence proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Full disclosure ordered subject to conditions that records not be shown to Samuel and that irrelevant personal information about his mother not be disclosed to her; each party to bear own costs.
enrichment.ratio: Pre-action disclosure may be ordered where likely issues and documents are sufficiently focused; confidentiality and Article 8 interests of third parties must be balanced against the public interest in fair administration of justice, and a data controller raising a valid objection should indicate how it can properly be met.
legal_issues: Whether CPR 31.16 pre-action disclosure criteria were satisfied
Whether disclosure should be limited to protect Samuel from harm
How to balance third-party confidentiality and Article 8 rights
Which party bears costs where opposition was partly reasonable
linked_authorities: Moresfield Ltd v Barnes [2003] EWHC 1602 (Ch)
Campbell v Enfield London Borough Council [1982] QB 1065
R (S) v Plymouth City Council [2002] 1 WLR 2583

confidence.notes: Disclosure order and conditions are explicit; parties were anonymised in the judgment.

notes: Landmark ERA age-limit indirect discrimination appeal; Seymour-Smith pool analysis is central and clear.

enrichment.short_title: Rutherford: ERA upper age limit and indirect sex discrimination under Article 141
key_facts: Two male employees over 65 claimed unfair dismissal and redundancy pay after dismissal in 1998 and 2001.
The employment tribunal disapplied the default age 65 exclusions in sections 109 and 156 ERA as indirectly discriminatory against men.
Statistical evidence compared disadvantaged age bands rather than the whole workforce.
The Secretary of State became involved because both employers were insolvent.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from the Employment Appeal Tribunal allowing the Secretary of State's appeal against tribunal jurisdiction findings.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals dismissed; the age 65 limit did not have disparate adverse impact on men when the correct Seymour-Smith pool was used, so objective justification did not arise.
enrichment.ratio: Indirect sex discrimination under Article 141 requires comparison of the proportions of men and women in the entire workforce who can comply with a neutral requirement; focusing only on those disadvantaged by an upper age limit is legally erroneous following Seymour-Smith.
legal_issues: Definition of the relevant pool for assessing disparate adverse impact
Whether the Burden of Proof Directive alters the Seymour-Smith methodology
Whether the age 65 cap was objectively justifiable social policy
Whether government witness statements could establish justification
linked_authorities: R v Secretary of State for Employment ex p Seymour-Smith [1999] ICR 447
R v Secretary of State for Employment ex p Equal Opportunities Commission [1995] 1 AC 1
Marshall v Southampton and SW Hampshire Health Authority [1986] ICR 335

confidence.notes: Core pool-definition issue and dismissal are comprehensively reasoned across a long judgment.

notes: IHT lease/settlement set-aside on mistake; Gibbon v Mitchell application and findings are clear.

enrichment.short_title: Wolff v Wolff: set-aside of reversionary lease in inheritance tax scheme
key_facts: Mr and Mrs Wolff granted a 125-year reversionary lease to their daughters and executed a defective trust deed as part of an IHT saving scheme.
They understood the arrangement as a paper exercise allowing them to remain in the house paying peppercorn rent.
From 2017 the lease would deprive them of occupation rights, which they had not appreciated and could not afford to remedy by paying market rent.
The solicitor Mr Kingshill had poorly understood and drafted the scheme documents.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Part 8 claim for declarations and orders setting aside voluntary lease and settlement where defendants did not oppose.
enrichment.outcome: Reversionary lease set aside for mistake as to its effect; trust deed point became academic; lease would not have been held on settlement trusts.
enrichment.ratio: A voluntary disposition may be set aside where the disponor's mistake is as to the legal effect of the transaction itself, not merely its commercial consequences; believing a future lease would not affect free occupation was such a mistake under Gibbon v Mitchell.
legal_issues: Whether the Wolffs' misunderstanding was mistake as to effect or mere consequence
Whether inadequate solicitor explanation supported a separate set-aside ground
Whether the trust deed gave daughters capital interests as intended
Whether the lease was held on the trusts of the settlement
linked_authorities: Gibbon v Mitchell [1990] 1 WLR 1304
AMP (UK) plc v Barker [2001] PLR 77
Philippson v Kerry (1863) 32 Beav 628

confidence.notes: Findings on misunderstanding and set-aside order are detailed though witness evidence was untested.

notes: Unusual costs appeal where Recorder corrected intended one-third trial costs order.

enrichment.short_title: Gordon v Harry: correction of confused county court costs order
key_facts: Miss Gordon and Mr Harry were joint owners of a cohabited property; she sought sale and a declared share reflecting her 28% contribution.
The Recorder ordered sale with proceeds held equally and made Mr Harry pay her costs save two-thirds of trial costs.
Mr Harry appealed out of time after receiving a substantial bill of costs; the Recorder later said he had meant one-third not two-thirds.
Each party's credibility was heavily criticised; Mr Harry won on beneficial shares but lost on resisting sale.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal out of time against a county court costs order, with appeal following if granted.
enrichment.outcome: Time extended, permission granted, and appeal allowed; Mr Harry to pay costs of the action but only one-third of trial costs instead of two-thirds.
enrichment.ratio: Where a trial judge has materially erred in exercising costs discretion through self-confessed confusion, the Court of Appeal may intervene and re-exercise discretion; a party who wins on the main issue at trial is prima facie entitled to costs of days on which that issue was tried.
legal_issues: Whether extension of time to appeal should be granted
Whether the Recorder's two-thirds trial costs order was a material discretion error
Whether the Court of Appeal could re-exercise discretion on trial costs
Whether the Recorder could revise his perfected order after losing jurisdiction

confidence.notes: Costs outcome and Recorder's corrected intention are clearly documented in transcript and letter.

notes: Fresh asylum claim JR; Rule 346, credibility and fabricated documents analysis is thorough.

enrichment.short_title: Gungor: judicial review of refusal to treat further representations as fresh asylum claim
key_facts: A Turkish Kurd entered on a forged visa, claimed asylum, and was refused after a fast-track appeal dismissed for lack of credibility.
Further documents including an HADEP application, arrest warrant and identity card were submitted as a fresh claim.
The adjudicator had found fabrication of the account, passport misuse, and inconsistent dates for key incidents.
The Secretary of State's April 2004 decision rejected the material as not credible or sufficiently different under Rule 346.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of refusal to treat post-appeal representations as a fresh asylum application under Rule 346.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; Secretary of State lawfully concluded the new material was unavailable, not credible and insufficiently different to meet paragraph 334.
enrichment.ratio: Under Rule 346 and Onibiyo, availability is a weighty factor but not decisive where ignoring credible new evidence would risk breaching human rights; here the documents were inconsistent with prior evidence and bore signs of fabrication.
legal_issues: Application of Rule 346(i)-(iii) to allegedly fresh asylum material
Interaction of Ladd v Marshall, Haile and E v Secretary of State principles
Whether age and passport evidence undermined the original refusal
Costs consequences of late service of the Secretary of State's fresh decision
linked_authorities: R v Secretary of State for the Home Department ex p Onibiyo [1996] 2 All ER 901
R (Haile) v Immigration Appeal Tribunal [2002] INLR 283
E v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2004] EWCA Civ 49

confidence.notes: Final disposition on fresh claim law and document credibility is clearly stated.

notes: Rare s41A undertakings-in-lieu case; GMC extension application dismissed with undertakings accepted.

enrichment.short_title: GMC v Mehrotra: undertakings accepted instead of extending interim conditions
key_facts: Dr Mehrotra faced GMC proceedings after a missed breast cancer on a mammogram in October 2002.
The Interim Orders Committee imposed 18-month conditions including a ban on mammogram reporting and employer notification requirements.
The GMC applied to extend the order for 12 months because the substantive hearing was adjourned to January 2005.
Dr Mehrotra offered court undertakings mirroring the conditions and contended the stigma of an order was unnecessary.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court application under section 41A(6)-(7) of the Medical Act 1983 to extend interim conditional registration imposed by the GMC.
enrichment.outcome: GMC application dismissed; court accepted voluntary undertakings in lieu of extension as a rare case where public protection did not require a continued order.
enrichment.ratio: Section 41A anticipates court extension of IOC orders so review and breach powers remain; undertakings in lieu should rarely be accepted, but may be appropriate where an unblemished practitioner credibly offers equivalent conditions and no breach is anticipated.
legal_issues: Whether undertakings can replace a section 41A extension order
Whether breach of undertakings would amount to serious professional misconduct
Whether the assessment panel report justified continued conditions
Costs where undertakings were offered before the hearing

confidence.notes: Discretionary outcome and limitation to unusual facts are expressly stated.

notes: Patent confidentiality club application refused for lack of evidence of need in English proceedings.

enrichment.short_title: Halliburton v Smith: refusal to widen patent litigation confidentiality club
key_facts: Halliburton and Smith compete in drill-bit design with parallel patent litigation in England, the US and Italy.
Smith served a confidential product and process description in English proceedings with an agreed core confidentiality club.
Halliburton sought to add US and Italian lawyers and engineers to the club for cross-jurisdictional consistency.
Shortly before the hearing Halliburton narrowed the application to four named foreign lawyers.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interlocutory application to expand a confidentiality club governing disclosure of a product and process description in patent infringement proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; no sufficient evidence that the four additional individuals were needed for proper conduct of the English proceedings.
enrichment.ratio: A party seeking to expand a confidentiality club must show why additional personnel will significantly contribute to fair conduct of the English case; fear of inconsistent foreign litigation or logistical convenience without evidence is insufficient.
legal_issues: Whether the product and process description contained confidential information
Whether foreign lawyers needed access for English proceedings
Whether inconsistent cases abroad justified club expansion
Evidentiary burden on applicant for confidentiality club membership

confidence.notes: Interlocutory refusal and reasoning on evidential burden are explicit.

notes: Leading CPR 35 point on privilege in earlier expert reports; appeal dismissed clearly.

enrichment.short_title: Jackson v Marley Davenport: privilege in earlier expert pathology reports
key_facts: Mr Jackson suffered severe head and spinal injuries falling at a German construction site in September 1999.
Professor Rutty prepared an April 2004 report for a lawyers' conference and a June 2004 report served as trial evidence.
The defendants applied for disclosure of the earlier report after noticing Rutty referred to additional information.
District Judge Mort ordered disclosure; HHJ Hull allowed the claimant's appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from refusal to order disclosure of an expert's earlier report and from an order requiring fuller instruction disclosure under CPR 35.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; earlier expert reports prepared for legal advice remain protected by litigation privilege and CPR 35.13 does not require their disclosure.
enrichment.ratio: CPR 35.10(4) abrogates privilege only for material instructions underlying the expert's intended trial report; earlier draft or preliminary expert reports created for legal advice or conference remain privileged and need not be disclosed under CPR 35.13.
legal_issues: Whether CPR 35.13 overrides litigation privilege in earlier expert reports
Distinction between instructions and earlier drafts under CPR 35.10
Whether partial disclosure of expert evidence is permitted
Application of Carlson v Townsend to expert reports
linked_authorities: Carlson v Townsend [2001] 1 WLR 2415
Lucas v Barking, Havering and Redbridge Hospitals NHS Trust [2004] 1 WLR 220

confidence.notes: Point of principle and unanimous dismissal are clearly articulated.

notes: Sentencing guidance for addict undercover-supply cases; three appeals partially allowed with revised tariffs.

enrichment.short_title: R v Afonso: sentencing addict retail suppliers of Class A drugs to undercover police
key_facts: The Court of Appeal heard three appeals together concerning retail supply of Class A drugs to undercover officers.
The court reviewed whether Djahit and Twisse six-year tariffs were disproportionate for unemployed addicts supplying only police with no stock.
Afonso supplied heroin and crack over about ten days; Sajid supplied with a co-accused Jamil; Andrews had demonstrable stock.
New guidance suggested about two to two-and-a-half years after a guilty plea for first-time adult offenders in the core category.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Three appeals against sentence with the court issuing revised sentencing guidance for a subgroup of retail Class A suppliers.
enrichment.outcome: Guidance issued reducing tariffs for addict suppliers to undercover police only; Afonso reduced to three-and-a-half years, Sajid to two-and-a-half years, Andrews to four years.
enrichment.ratio: For out-of-work addicts whose sole motive is funding their addiction, who hold no stock and are shown only to have supplied undercover police, Djahit/Twisse levels are disproportionate; such first-time adult offenders should generally receive about two to two-and-a-half years after a timely guilty plea.
legal_issues: Whether Djahit and Twisse tariffs should be revised downward for a subgroup
When drug treatment and testing orders are appropriate
Distinction between commercial dealers and addict suppliers to police
Disparity and role in multi-defendant supply cases
linked_authorities: R v Djahit [1999] 2 Cr App R (S) 142
R v Twisse [2001] 2 Cr App R (S) 37
Attorney-General's Reference No 64 of 2003 [2004] 2 Cr App R (S) 106

confidence.notes: Guidance and individual sentence reductions are clearly stated with limiting qualifications.

notes: Costs master ruling on regulation 10 procedure; Jeyeanthan/Howard analysis applied to statement of resources omission.

enrichment.short_title: Cafane v Lambeth: whether failure to file statement of resources nullifies s.11 costs application
key_facts: Mrs Cafane, a legally aided claimant, lost a disrepair/right-to-buy trial and was ordered to pay Lambeth's costs under section 11 of the Access to Justice Act 1999.
Lambeth applied within three months for assessment of the claimant's means and a costs order against the Legal Services Commission, giving written notice but without filing a statement of resources.
The Commission applied to set aside the directions on the basis that no valid application against it had been made and that the omission of a statement of resources was fatal.
Master Gordon-Saker held the request was a valid section 11 application against the Commission but that failure to file or serve a statement of resources was directory, not a nullity.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application by the Legal Services Commission to set aside costs assessment directions made on Lambeth's section 11 application.
enrichment.outcome: The Commission's application was dismissed; the defendant's request for a hearing to determine costs was effective despite the missing statement of resources.
enrichment.ratio: Under regulation 10 of the Community Legal Service (Costs) Regulations 2000, failure to accompany a timely request for a section 11 costs hearing with a statement of resources does not render the proceedings a nullity; applying Jeyeanthan and Howard, such procedural requirements are directory and the court should consider substantial compliance and just consequences rather than treating any breach as jurisdictional.
legal_issues: Whether Lambeth's application constituted a valid request for a costs order against the Commission under regulation 10
Whether failure to file a statement of resources with the request rendered the application a nullity
Whether Jones v Zahedi and Middleton require automatic rejection for non-compliance
Whether the court has power to extend time for filing a statement of resources
linked_authorities: Jones v Zahedi [1993] 1 WLR 1445
Middleton v Middleton [1994] unrep 14 December
R v Secretary of State for the Home Department ex parte Jeyeanthan [2000] 1 WLR 354
Howard v Secretary of State for the Environment [1975] 1 QB 235
R v Greenwich London Borough Council ex parte Lovelace (No 2) [1992] 1 All ER 679
